u-thant: Thant was born on 22 January 1909 in Pantanaw, Burma, then a province of British India, the eldest of four sons of Po Hnit, who had been educated in Calcutta. After Po Hnit died when Thant was fourteen, inheritance disputes left the family in difficulty. Thant took a two-year teaching certificate at Rangoon University in 1926, where he studied history alongside the future Prime Minister U Nu, who became a close friend. He taught at the National High School in Pantanaw from 1928 and became its headmaster at twenty-five.

During the Japanese occupation from 1942 to 1945 he defied an order to teach Japanese and cooperated with the resistance. After independence in 1948 Nu appointed him director of broadcasting, and from 1951 to 1957 he served as secretary to the prime minister. He was secretary of the 1955 Bandung Conference and from 1957 Burma's permanent representative to the United Nations.

Dag Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash in September 1961, and on 3 November the Security Council recommended Thant, whom the General Assembly appointed unanimously. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, on 20 October 1962 President Kennedy showed him aerial photographs of Soviet missile installations. Thant proposed that the United States give non-invasion guarantees in exchange for the removal of the missiles, and Khrushchev welcomed the proposal. In December 1962 he ordered Operation Grandslam, which ended the Katanga secession in the Congo.

He was reappointed on 2 December 1966, and dozens of newly independent Asian and African states entered the UN in his second term. He publicly criticised the American conduct of the Vietnam War, and was criticised in the United States and Israel for withdrawing UNEF from the Sinai in 1967 at Egypt's request. He refused a third term and retired in 1971.

Thant died of lung cancer in New York on 25 November 1974. Burma was by then ruled by a military junta under Ne Win, which refused him any honours. On 5 December tens of thousands lined the streets of Rangoon for his funeral, and students seized the coffin and buried it on the grounds of the Rangoon University Students Union. On 12 December government troops removed it and reburied it near the Shwedagon Pagoda; riots followed and martial law was declared. This is known as the U Thant crisis.

Chairman Gunnar Jahn of the Nobel committee prevented the Peace Prize going to Thant in 1965, and none was awarded in 1966 or 1967. His grandson, the historian Thant Myint-U, wrote of him in The River of Lost Footsteps.
ubaid-period: The name comes from Tell al-'Ubaid, where the earliest large excavation of Ubaid material was begun by Henry Hall in 1919, followed by Leonard Woolley in 1922–1923 and Pinhas Delougaz in 1937. Excavators at Eridu and Tell al-'Ubaid first found the pottery in the 1910s and 1920s, and in 1930 a conference in Baghdad defined an Ubaid pottery style of black-on-buff painted ware. Joan Oates showed in 1960 that the Eridu and Hajji Muhammed styles belonged to the same Ubaid phenomenon, and proposed a framework of four phases, to which other scholars later added two more.

The oldest known Ubaid site is Tell el-'Oueili in the south. No site in southern Iraq has yielded remains older than the Ubaid, though earlier ones may lie buried under alluvial sediment. In central and northern Iraq the Ubaid followed the Hassuna and Samarra cultures, and in northern Syria and southeastern Turkey it followed the Halaf period.

Ubaid and Ubaid-like material has been found over a vast area, with pottery from Mersin in the west to Tepe Ghabristan in the east, and south to Dosariyah on the Gulf coast of Saudi Arabia. Researchers see considerable regional variation, so the Ubaid was not a single culture across time and space. Pottery reached the Persian Gulf coast toward the end of the sixth millennium BCE, at sites such as Bahra 1 and H3 in Kuwait and Dalma Island, and may have been a valued trade item, perhaps exchanged for fish, dates or shell jewellery.

Villages were large and unwalled, with multi-roomed rectangular mud-brick houses and the first temples of public architecture in Mesopotamia. Settlements formed two tiers, with large centres of more than ten hectares among smaller villages. Farmers grew barley, wheat, lentils and flax, and southern agriculture used irrigation and the plough, perhaps introduced from the north. The period gives the first evidence for boating in the Near East, in ceramic boat models, some showing reed boats and others masts. Evidence for wool is mostly indirect, and copper objects, found at northern sites late in the period, remain rare.

Burials were mostly primary inhumations, often with beads, pots and red ochre. Many people practised circumferential headshaping, which elongated the skull, and wore labrets or ear-spools, both interpreted as markers of group identity. Figurines include animals and mostly female human figures, among them the slender so-called ophidian figures found only in the south.

The languages spoken in the period cannot be determined, yet it has featured in the debate about the Sumerian language. In the 1930s Henri Frankfort proposed that Sumerian speakers came from the Iranian highlands at the start of the Ubaid, while E. A. Speiser thought they arrived during the Uruk period. In the south the Ubaid was succeeded by the Uruk period.
ubs: UBS has two main predecessors. The older, the Swiss Bank Corporation, began in 1854 when six private banking firms in Basel pooled their resources as the Bankverein, a consortium that acted as an underwriting syndicate for its members. In 1871 it joined the German Frankfurter Bankverein to form the joint-stock Basler Bankverein, which suspended its dividend until 1879 after heavy losses in Germany. Following mergers in 1885 and 1886 it became the Schweizerischer Bankverein, and in 1917 its English name was changed to Swiss Bank Corporation.

The Bank in Winterthur was founded in 1862 with a share capital of CHF 5 million to finance industry. It profited from its railroad connections and warehouses during the American Civil War, when cotton prices rose sharply. In 1912 it fused with the Toggenburger Bank, a savings and mortgage bank founded in 1863 with a branch network in eastern Switzerland. The merged firm took the name Union Bank of Switzerland in 1921.

In the mid-1990s Union Bank of Switzerland came under fire from dissident shareholders who criticised its conservative management. Martin Ebner, through his investment trust BK Vision, became its largest shareholder and pressed for restructuring. Credit Suisse proposed a merger in 1996, which the board rejected unanimously, but Ebner led a shareholder revolt that replaced the chairman, Robert Studer, with Mathis Cabiallavetta, one of the architects of the merger with the Swiss Bank Corporation. The merger took place in 1998.

On 3 November 2000 UBS merged with the American brokerage Paine Webber, and in 2003 the name Paine Webber disappeared in favour of the single UBS brand. At the beginning of 2007 UBS was the first Wall Street firm to announce a heavy loss in the subprime mortgage sector, and during the financial crisis in 2008 GIC Private Limited invested CHF 11 billion in it. In March 2023 UBS agreed to buy Credit Suisse in an emergency rescue deal, which it completed on 12 June 2023.

UBS is a joint-stock company under Swiss law, with its headquarters in both Zurich and Basel. Its business covers wealth management, asset management, investment banking and banking for private and corporate clients in Switzerland. The bank draws on Swiss traditions of privacy. Banking secrecy goes back to the 1700s, and the Federal Act on Banks and Savings Banks of 1934 criminalised giving client information to third parties. Its secrecy practices have led to disputes with foreign tax authorities, and UBS reached agreements with the United States tax service in 2009 and with U.K. HM Revenue and Customs in 2010.
udaipur: Udaipur lies in the southernmost part of Rajasthan near the Gujarat border, on the south slope of the Aravalli Range, which separates it from the Thar Desert. It stands at 598 metres above sea level and covers 64 square kilometres. Its lakes form an interconnected system fed by the Berach river and its tributaries. The city lakes include Lake Pichola, Fateh Sagar Lake, Swaroop Sagar Lake and Rang Sagar, and downstream lies Udaisagar Lake. Because of its lakes it is sometimes called the Venice of the East, and the British administrator James Tod called it the most romantic spot on the continent of India.

Maharana Udai Singh II of the Sisodia clan of Rajputs founded Udaipur in 1559, as the new capital of Mewar. He was the father of Maharana Pratap. The area already held a trading town, Ayad, which had been the capital of Mewar from the 10th to the 12th centuries. After the rise of artillery warfare in the 16th century, Udai Singh decided during his exile at Kumbhalgarh Fort to move to a more secure site. Ayad was flood-prone, so he chose the ridge east of Lake Pichola. In the legend, a hermit he met while hunting blessed him and told him to build a palace there.

The Mughal emperor Akbar conquered Chittor in November 1567. To protect his territory, Udai Singh built a six-kilometre city wall with gates including Surajpole, Chandpole, Hathipole and Delhi Gate. The area within is still known as the old city. Udaipur remained the capital of Mewar until 1818, when Mewar became a British princely state, and Mewar became part of Rajasthan after India's independence.

Udaipur is the administrative headquarters of Udaipur district, about 415 kilometres south of the state capital Jaipur. Hindi and Mewari are its major languages. The 2011 census gave the city 451,100 inhabitants. Its economy rests on tourism, agriculture and mineral industries, and it is known for marble, silver, paintings and terracotta. Visitors come for the lakes, palaces, forts and temples, and for festivals such as Gangaur, which women celebrate in the month of Chaitra and whose idols are immersed in Lake Pichola from the Gangaur Ghat.
udine: Udine stands in the middle of the historical region of Friuli, a little over 20 kilometres from Slovenia, between the Cormor stream to the west and the Torre stream to the east. It lies at the crossing of east-west and north-south routes. At its centre is an isolated hill crowned by the castle. Legend says Attila the Hun raised the hill to watch the burning of Aquileia, but excavations show that it is artificial and holds no rock.

The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic. Udine is first mentioned in 983, when Emperor Otto II gave the castle of Utinum to the Patriarchs of Aquileia, then the main feudal lords of the region. From 1222 it was one of their residences, after Bertoldo of Andechs moved from Cividale following an earthquake. The foundation of the market in 1223 made it the most important city of the area for trade.

The Republic of Venice conquered it in 1420, and it stayed under Venetian control until 1797 as the state's second largest city. A short civil war in 1511 was followed by an earthquake and a plague. After the fall of Venice it passed to Austrian rule, then briefly to the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy, then back to the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia, and joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866. From May 1915 to October 1917 it was the seat of the Italian High Command, nicknamed the War Capital, and after Caporetto it was occupied by German and Austro-Hungarian forces.

Udine is the second-largest city of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. In its main square, Piazza della Libertà, stands the Loggia del Lionello, built from 1448 to 1457 in the Venetian Gothic style and rebuilt after a fire in 1876, opposite a clock tower resembling that of the Piazza San Marco. The cathedral was begun in 1236 and consecrated in 1335. Friulian is taught in the city's schools, and a small Slovene population lives near the border.
udmurts: The Udmurts are a Permian, Finno-Ugric people of Eastern Europe who speak the Udmurt language, a member of the Uralic family. Their name derives from a Permic form meaning meadow people, built from the root for meadow, glade or turf and murt, person, probably an early borrowing from an Iranian language. A document of 1557 calls them lugovye lyudi, 'meadow people', beside the traditional Russian name votyaki. Another theory derives the name wholly from Proto-Iranian, meaning resident of the outskirts or border zone.

Under the Russian Empire they were mainly called Chud Otyatskaya, Otyaks, Wotyaks or Votyaks. Udmurts today consider these names offensive. They are closely related to the Komis to their north, both in language and culture.

Most Udmurts live in Udmurtia in Russia, where they make up 24.1% of the population, with small groups in Kirov Oblast, Perm Krai, Bashkortostan, Tatarstan and Mari El. The Russian census counted 746,562 in 1989 and 552,299 in 2010.

The Udmurts used to be semi-nomadic forest dwellers living in riverside communities, but most now live in towns. Their clan-based social structure no longer exists, though its traces remain strong and continue to shape Udmurt culture. They have a national epic, Dorvyzhy, and national instruments include the krez, a zither similar to the Russian gusli, and a pipe-like wind instrument, the chipchirghan. A chapter of the 1776 book Description de toutes les nations de l'empire de Russie describes the Wotyak people, and James George Frazer mentions a rite of theirs in The Golden Bough. About 70% of Udmurt men carry haplogroup N, a pattern common among Uralic-speaking peoples.
udupi: Udupi is a city on the coast of Karnataka and the administrative headquarters of Udupi district, at an elevation of 27 metres. Its name may derive from the Sanskrit udupa, meaning moon, or from the Tulu odipu, meaning elevated land. Summers, from March to May, are hot, and the monsoon from June to September brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain a year. Kaup and Malpe are among the beaches, and the harbour of Malpe lies 5 kilometres away. The most spoken language is Tulu, with Kannada and Konkani also heard.

In the 13th century the Vaishnavite saint Madhvacharya founded the Sri Krishna Temple at Udupi and set up eight mathas, the Ashta Mathas, to propagate the Dvaita Vedanta philosophy. A vibrant temple culture took root in the district, and significant migration of Brahmins to the region followed, so that they came to make up about 10 per cent of its population, three times the proportion elsewhere in South India. The city is also known as Parashurama Kshetra.

Udupi cuisine is linked to the Krishna Matha. Krishna is offered food of many kinds every day, with restrictions on ingredients during Chaturmasa, the four months of the monsoon, and these restrictions together with the need for variety led to innovation with seasonal and local materials. The cuisine was developed by the Shivalli Madhwa Brahmins who cooked for Krishna, and at the Krishna Matha food is provided free of cost. Restaurants serving it are found in most large cities of India.

Udupi's cultural traditions include Bhuta Kola, Nagaradhane and the folk art of Yakshagana, and during Krishna Janmashtami the tiger dance Pili Yesa is performed in the streets. The economy rests on agriculture, fishing, small industries such as cashew processing, and a handloom sari industry. Manipal, a suburb, is known as an education and medical centre, and the Syndicate Bank and Corporation Bank were founded in Udupi. The city lies on the Konkan Railway, and National Highway 66 links it to Mangalore.
ufa: Ufa lies near the land boundary between Eastern Europe and Northern Asia, at the confluence of the Belaya, called Agidel in Bashkir, and the Ufa rivers. It stands on low hills forming the Ufa Plateau, west of the southern Ural Mountains, and stretches 53.5 kilometres from north to south. The name comes from the river, but the origin of the river's name is disputed: the linguist Aleksandr Matveyev proposed an Iranian origin, from a word for water.

Some accounts place a medieval city on the site from about the 5th to the 16th century. A town called Pascherti, meaning Bashkort, appears roughly on the Belaya on the Pizzigano brothers' map of 1367, the Catalan Atlas of 1375 and Gerardus Mercator's map of 1554, and Henri Cordier connected it with Ufa. Ibn Khaldun listed Bashkort among the largest cities of the Golden Horde, and the historian Peter Rychkov wrote that a great city stood there before the Russians came.

By order of Ivan the Terrible a fortress was built on the site in 1574, first named Tura-Tau after its hill; that year is now the official date of the city's foundation, and it received town status in 1586. Ufa became the seat of a separate governorate in 1781, and in 1802 the centre of the whole Orenburg Governorate. The Belaya River Waterway of 1870 and the Samara-Zlatoust Railroad of 1890 tied it to European Russia and encouraged light industry. After the Soviet retreat of 1941 many industrial enterprises from the west of the country were evacuated to Ufa.

Ufa is the capital and largest city of Bashkortostan, with over 1.1 million people, a majority of them ethnic Russians with substantial numbers of Bashkirs and Tatars. Its industry rests on oil refining, chemicals and mechanical engineering, and the oil company Bashneft has its headquarters there. The city has several universities, among them Bashkir State University, and lies on a historic branch of the Trans-Siberian Railway.
uglich: Uglich lies on the Volga River in Yaroslavl Oblast. It was first documented in 1148 as Ugliche Pole, meaning Corner Field. The name is thought to allude to a nearby turn in the Volga and derives from the Russian word ugol, a corner or nook.

From 1218 until 1328 Uglich was the seat of a small princedom, and the local princes then sold their rights to the great prince of Moscow. As a border town of the Grand Duchy of Moscow it was burned several times in conflicts with Lithuanians, Tatars and the grand prince of Tver. In 1462 Grand Duke Ivan III of Moscow gave the town to his younger brother Andrey Bolshoy. Under Andrey the town was expanded and its first stone buildings were raised, among them a cathedral, the Intercession Monastery and the red-brick palace of the prince, completed in 1481 and still standing.

Under Ivan the Terrible the town passed to his only brother, Yury. Its inhabitants helped the tsar to take Kazan by building a wooden fortress that was carried down the Volga to the city. Uglich prospered throughout the 16th century, after which its fortunes declined.

After Ivan's death his youngest son, Dmitry Ivanovich, was banished to Uglich in 1584. On 15 May 1591 the ten-year-old boy was found dead with his throat cut in the palace courtyard. Suspicion fell at once on the tsar's chief adviser, Boris Godunov, but official investigators concluded that the death was an accident. They also cut the tongue from the cathedral bell that had rung the news and sent it into exile in Siberia.

Dmitry was the last of the ancient Rurik dynasty, and his death is seen as a precipitating cause of the dynastic and political crisis known as the Time of Troubles. People readily believed he was alive and supported several False Dmitrys, each of whom tried to seize the Muscovite throne. During that crisis Poles besieged the Alexeievsky and Uleima monasteries and burned them, killing the people who had taken refuge inside.

The Romanov tsars soon had the boy canonised and made Uglich a place of pilgrimage. In 1690 the town built the small Church of St Demetrios on the Blood where he was thought to have been killed, and the palace became a museum. The image of the tsarevich with a knife in his hand was adopted as the town's coat of arms. The Assumption church of the Alexeyevsky Monastery, dated 1628, is regarded as a gem of medieval Russian architecture. Damming of the Volga in the 20th century, under Stalin, caused severe flooding of the town's outskirts.
uherske-hradiste: Uherské Hradiště lies on the left bank of the Morava River in the Zlín Region, about 23 km south-west of Zlín. Its western part lies in the Lower Morava Valley and its eastern part in the Vizovice Highlands, and the Olšava River flows through the south. The town forms one built-up area with its neighbours Staré Město and Kunovice. The name means Hungarian gord, a fortified settlement near the Hungarian border, and the town is the centre of the cultural region of Moravian Slovakia, known for its folklore, music, costumes and winemaking.

A predecessor of the town was a settlement and fortification system on three islands in the Morava, founded by Slavic tribes in the early 9th century. It disappeared after the fall of Great Moravia. The town itself was founded in 1257 by King Ottokar II to protect the nearby monastery at Velehrad. It was first called Nový Velehrad, meaning new Velehrad, then Hradiště, and the name Uherské Hradiště was first used in 1587.

In the 14th century stone walls replaced the original wooden palisades, and the fortifications were improved over the following centuries. The town faced repeated raids: by the Cumans in the 16th century, in the fighting of the Thirty Years' War and by Turkish invasions during the Austro-Turkish War of 1716 to 1718. It was not conquered until 1742, by the Prussian army. The Jesuits worked there from 1644 to 1773 and founded a college, the Church of Saint Francis Xavier and a school. In the 1780s the town ceased to function as a fortress, and in the mid-19th century it began to grow beyond its walls.

The town has about 25,000 inhabitants, and the agglomeration with Staré Město and Kunovice over 37,000. Its well-preserved historic centre is protected as an urban monument zone. The main landmark of the square, Masarykovo náměstí, is the Baroque Church of Saint Francis Xavier, built in 1670 to 1685. The Franciscan monastery was founded in 1491, and the Moravian Slovakia Museum, one of the most popular ethnographic museums in Moravia, was founded in 1895. The synagogue of 1875 was burned in 1944, rebuilt after World War II and now serves as a library. The Summer Film School has been held in the town every year since 1992.
ujjain: Ujjain stands on the eastern bank of the Shipra River on the Malwa plateau, north of the upper limit of the Vindhya ranges, at an average elevation of 494 metres. In antiquity it was known as Avantika and also as Ujjayini, and the Arabs called it Uzayn. Chalcolithic farming settlements of about 2000 BCE have been found at Kayatha, some 26 kilometres away, though not at Ujjain itself. The Avanti region showed early signs of urbanisation around 700 BCE, and around 600 BCE Ujjain emerged as the political, commercial and cultural centre of the plateau.

The ancient walled city lay around the Garh Kalika hill. It covered an irregular pentagon of 0.875 square kilometres, with a mud rampart 12 metres high and a moat 45 metres wide, built between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE according to F. R. Allchin and George Erdosy. Avanti was one of the sixteen Mahājanapadas, with Ujjain as its capital. In the 4th century BCE Chandragupta annexed it to the Mauryan empire. Ashoka served as viceroy at Ujjain under his father Bindusara, and his edicts name it as the capital of the Western province. It lay on the trade route from Mathura to the Deccan and was a centre of learning for Jain, Buddhist and Hindu traditions.

Ujjain remained important under Gupta rule in the 4th and 5th centuries, and the poet Kalidasa refers to it many times and describes its wealth in the Meghadūta. The Umayyad Arabs sacked it several times in the 8th century. Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it, and Iltutmish of the Delhi Sultanate plundered it in 1235. In the Mughal period Jai Singh II built a Jantar Mantar there. Ranoji Scindia made it the capital of the Scindia state in 1731, and the Holkars defeated the Scindias at the Battle of Ujjain on 18 July 1801. After both accepted British suzerainty, British administrators chose to develop Indore as an alternative to Ujjain.

Ujjain is a city in Ujjain district in Madhya Pradesh and is one of the Hindu pilgrimage centres of the Sapta Puri. According to Puranic legend, it is one of four sites where drops of amrita fell from a pitcher during the churning of the ocean of milk, and the Kumbh Mela, or Simhastha, is held there every 12 years. The temple of Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga stands at the centre of the city. Bathing in the Shipra is believed to free a person from sins, so Ujjain is also called the city that gives liberation. Hindi is the most spoken language, and Malvi is widely spoken.
ukiyo-e: In 1603 Edo became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, and the chōnin class of merchants, craftsmen and workers, at the bottom of the social order, gained most from the city's rapid economic growth. They patronised kabuki theatre, geisha and the courtesans of the pleasure districts, and the term ukiyo came to describe this hedonistic way of life. Painted hanging scrolls known as Portraits of Kanbun Beauties gained popularity around 1661 and marked the beginnings of ukiyo-e as an independent school.

The earliest ukiyo-e works emerged in the 1670s, with the paintings and monochrome prints of beautiful women by Hishikawa Moronobu. Scholars disagree whether the paintings of Iwasa Matabei belong to the genre, and Japanese researchers in particular often name him as its founder rather than Moronobu.

Colour was at first added by hand for special commissions. In 1744 the benizuri-e became the first successes in colour printing, using one woodblock for each colour. Okumura Masanobu, who opened a shop in 1707, introduced geometrical perspective to the uki-e genre in the 1740s, and in the 1760s the success of Suzuki Harunobu's brocade prints made full-colour production standard, with ten or more blocks for each print.

Production was divided among four groups: the publisher, who financed and distributed the prints, the artist, who made the design, the woodcarver and the printer. The artist's ink drawing was pasted to a block of cherry wood and cut away, so the original drawing was destroyed. Prints were impressed on hand-made paper by hand, which allowed gradations of colour that machines could not achieve. Typical subjects were beauties, kabuki actors, sumo wrestlers and, late in the tradition, landscapes.

A law of 1790 required prints to carry a censor's seal. Censorship grew stricter, and Utamaro was imprisoned in 1804 for prints of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The Tenpō Reforms of 1841 to 1843 suppressed images of courtesans and actors, so artists turned to travel scenes and to birds and flowers.

Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa and Hiroshige's The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō belong to the 19th century. After the deaths of both masters and the Meiji Restoration of 1868, ukiyo-e declined sharply: woodblock printing turned to journalism and faced competition from photography, and by the 1890s the tradition was moribund.

In the West, Carl Peter Thunberg was one of the earliest collectors of Japanese prints, and from the 1870s Japonisme influenced Edgar Degas, Édouard Manet, Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh. In 1915 the publisher Shōzaburō Watanabe introduced the term shin-hanga, new prints, for a revival that followed.
ukraine: Ukraine is the second-largest country in Europe after Russia and the largest entirely in Europe, covering 603,550 square kilometres with a coastline of 2,782 kilometres. It lies mostly in the East European Plain, and its landscape consists mostly of fertile steppes and plateaus crossed by rivers such as the Dnieper, the Dniester and the Southern Bug, which flow south to the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. The only mountains are the Carpathian Mountains in the west, of which the highest is Hoverla at 2,061 metres, and the Crimean Mountains in the extreme south. Significant natural resources include lithium, natural gas, kaolin, timber and abundant arable land.

Settlement by modern humans in Ukraine dates back to 32,000 BCE, and by 4,500 BCE the Neolithic Cucuteni–Trypillia culture was flourishing in wide areas. In the Iron Age the Cimmerians, Scythians and Sarmatians lived there. From the 6th century BCE Greek, Roman and Byzantine colonies such as Olbia and Chersonesus were established on the Black Sea shore. Kievan Rus' emerged in the 9th century, became the largest and most powerful realm in Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries, and was destroyed by the Mongols in the 13th century.

For the next 600 years the area was contested, divided and ruled by external powers including the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, the Kingdom of Poland, the Ottoman Empire and the Tsardom of Russia. The Cossack Hetmanate emerged in the 17th century and was gradually absorbed by the Russian Empire in the 18th century. The short-lived Ukrainian People's Republic was formed after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic became a constituent republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. In the early 1930s millions of Ukrainians died in the Holodomor, a human-made famine. During World War II Ukraine was occupied by Germany and endured major battles and atrocities, resulting in 7 million civilians killed, including most Ukrainian Jews.

Ukraine gained independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union dissolved, and adopted its constitution on 28 June 1996. Kyiv is the capital and largest city, and the official language is Ukrainian. The Orange Revolution of 2004 to 2005 and the Euromaidan of 2014 followed. Before 2022 the population was estimated at over 41 million.
ukrainians: The East Slavs emerged from the early Slavs in the migrations of the 6th and 7th centuries, and the state of Kievan Rus' united them from the 9th to the 13th century. East Slavic tribes called proto-Ukrainian include the Volhynians, Derevlianians, Polianians and Siverianians, and the Polianians are identified as the founders of Kiev. Varangians from Scandinavia conquered the tribes in the 9th century and laid the groundwork for the state. The Mongol invasions of 1236 and 1240 destroyed it, and the Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia (1199–1349) followed.

The Cossacks of Zaporizhzhia controlled the lower Dnieper from the late 15th century. Bohdan Khmelnytsky formed the Cossack Hetmanate (1648–1782), and in the Ruin of the late 17th century Ukraine split into hostile Left-Bank and Right-Bank halves. Under the Russian Empire Ukrainians were called Little Russians and Ukrainian was outlawed in almost all contexts. Ivan Kotliarevsky's Eneyida of 1798 established the modern language, and a Romantic revival followed.

In 1918 the Central Rada under Mykhailo Hrushevsky declared the independence of the Ukrainian National Republic. In 1932 and 1933 millions starved in the Holodomor, which Ukraine and many foreign governments and scholars have called genocide; scholarly estimates of the direct loss of life range from 2.6 million to 12 million. Independent Ukraine arose in 1991.

The name Ukraintsi comes from Ukraina, first documented in the Kievan Chronicle under 1187. Ukrainian, written in a Cyrillic alphabet, descends from the Old East Slavic of Kievan Rus', and most Ukrainians adhere to Eastern Orthodox Christianity. The name came into use in central Ukraine first and in Galicia and Bukovina only late in the 19th century. Sub-groups in the west, such as the Hutsuls, Boykos and Lemkos, keep their own dialects, dress and folk traditions. A diaspora lives in more than 120 countries.
ulaanbaatar: Ulaanbaatar lies at about 1,300 metres above sea level in a valley on the Tuul River, at the foot of Bogd Khan Mountain, which rises to 2,250 metres to the south and marks the boundary between the steppe zone and the forest-steppe zone to the north. Xiongnu-era royal tombs have been found around the city. Its elevation, latitude and distance from any coast make it the coldest national capital in the world.

The settlement began in 1639 as a yurt monastery called Örgöö, intended as the seat of Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu. It moved 29 times before it was permanently settled at its present site in 1778. By 1651 it was called Nomiin Khüree, and by 1706 Ikh Khüree. After the Treaty of Kyakhta in 1727 it became a major point of the Kyakhta trade between Russia and China, mostly Siberian furs for Chinese cloth and later tea.

In 1911, with the Qing dynasty collapsing, Mongolian leaders who had come to Ikh Khüree for Naadam met in secret on Mount Bogd Khan Uul and resolved to end 220 years of Manchu control. Soviet-style blocks of flats replaced most of the old ger districts from the 1950s, and the Trans-Mongolian Railway to Moscow and Beijing was completed in 1956. Most older temples and monasteries were destroyed in the purges of the late 1930s. Demonstrations in Sükhbaatar Square from 10 December 1989 led the governing party to resign on 9 March 1990, and a new constitution followed in 1992.

Ulaanbaatar is the capital and largest city of Mongolia, home to almost half of the country's population, and is governed as an independent first-level region separate from the surrounding Töv Province. It is divided into nine districts. The Choijin Lama Monastery, completed in 1908 and turned into a museum in 1942, and the Gandan Monastery, with its 26.5-metre statue of Migjid Janraisig, escaped the destruction of monasteries.
ulama: The ʿulamā, literally the learned ones, are scholars and judges of Islamic doctrine and law, regarded as the guardians, transmitters and interpreters of religious knowledge. The term can mean the educated class of theologians, muftis, qadis and professors, or specifically those holding government positions in an Islamic state. According to Tamim Ansary, the group began with the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, who funded a group of Muslims to study the revelations and the stories of Muhammad's life so that he could draw on their advice. Early jurists were concerned more with authority and teaching than with theory, until Muhammad ibn Idris ash-Shafi'i, who lived from 767 to 820, codified the principles of jurisprudence in his book ar-Risālah.

Students traditionally sought out leading teachers rather than a particular institution, and a teacher gave a finished scholar an ijaza, a licence to teach and to issue legal opinions. The madrasa, which probably originated in Khurasan in the 10th century, spread from the late 11th century. The best-known early ones were the Niẓāmiyyas, founded in the 11th century by the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk. The Mustansiriyya Madrasa, founded in Baghdad in 1234, was the first founded by a caliph and the first known to host teachers of all four major Sunni schools of law.

By the eleventh century the major schools of law had emerged, among them the Shafi'i, Maliki, Hanafi and Hanbali among Sunni schools, and the Ja'fari and Zaidi among Shia schools. Shared training in Arabic, and later Persian, let scholars move across the Islamic world. Ibn Battuta, born in Tangiers into a family of ulama, was made a qadi by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq of Delhi, and Nuruddin ar-Raniri, from a Gujarati family, became Shaykh ul-Islam under the Sultan of Aceh.

According to Feldman, under many caliphates and sultanates the ulama guarded Islamic law and kept the ruler from dictating legal outcomes, a sort of separation of powers. The Ottoman and Safavid empires both relied on ulama to legitimise their rule. Süleyman I integrated the imperial ulama into the bureaucracy and Ottoman secular law into Islamic law, but Shah Abbas I could not win the same support from the Shia ulama, who stayed independent. The Ottoman ulama opposed Selim III's army reforms as apostasy, and the reforms failed. In the 19th century a ministry of religious endowments reduced their control of finances and so their political influence.

Rifa'a al-Tahtawi stayed in Paris from 1826 to 1831, among the first ulama to travel to Europe. In the 20th century Kemalist Turkey distanced itself from the religious institutions of the Ottoman past, while Nasser increased state control of al-Azhar University from 1961.
ulcinj: Ulcinj is an ancient seaport, and the wider area has been inhabited since the Bronze Age, judging by Illyrian tombs found at Zogaj nearby. The town is believed to have been founded in the 5th century BCE by colonists from Colchis, as a poem of Apollonius of Rhodes mentions, and traces of Cyclopean walls remain visible in the old citadel. Ancient writers know it as Olcinium. Under Roman rule it received the status of a settlement of Roman citizens and was later granted municipium status. From around 820 it was the see of a diocese, suppressed in 1532 and revived as a Latin titular bishopric.

In the Middle Ages the Byzantine Empire held it, and in 1010 Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria failed to take it. Stefan Vojislav of Duklja conquered the region by 1040, and Stefan Nemanja took Ulcinj in 1183, after which it prospered as one of the most significant coastal towns. Later the Balšić family held it and minted coins there. The Republic of Venice captured it in 1405, and in 1571 it fell to the Ottoman Empire with the aid of North African corsairs after the Battle of Lepanto.

Under the Ottomans it gradually became Muslim-majority, and hammams, mosques and a clock tower were built. Piracy continued until Mehmed Pasha Bushati ended it. In the 19th century the port flourished again, and the geographer Antonio Baldacci reported a merchant marine of 500 ships.

After the Congress of Berlin redrew the borders between Montenegro and the Ottoman Empire, Muslim Albanian resistance prevented Montenegro from taking over Plav and Gusinje. The Great Powers decided in 1880 to reverse that transfer and offered Ulcinj, then also called Dulcigno, as compensation. The Ottoman Empire refused at first, and in May 1880 Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy and Russia organised a naval demonstration off the coast until it agreed to cede the town in exchange for compensation. About 3,000 of its 8,000 inhabitants, Albanians, left for northern Albania, and 142 Montenegrin families settled on the outskirts in the 1880s.

Ulcinj is the capital of Ulcinj Municipality and the centre of the Albanian community in Montenegro. Its urban population is 11,488. Its old town is a citadel on a rocky bluff above the shore, and Ulcinj Castle has parts that date back two millennia. There are 26 mosques in the town and the surrounding countryside, and Pasha's Mosque, the Sailors' Mosque and St. Nicholas' Church are among its religious buildings. Velika plaža is a sandy beach about 12 kilometres long, the longest on the Montenegrin coast. Montenegro became independent in 2006 after a referendum.
ulfilas: Ulfilas, also called Wulfila, was born around 311, presumably in what is now Romania. He was partly descended from Roman prisoners taken from Asia Minor in a Gothic raid on Sadagolthina, probably in 264 or 267 and carried to an area near the Danube. His ancestors were probably Christians, and he was raised as a Christian in a pagan society, within a community of Cappadocian Christians living under the Thervingi between the Olt, the Dniester and the Danube. He is believed to have been Cappadocian Greek on his mother's side and of Gothic descent through his father. No sources describe his education, but by age thirty he was a lector in a church in Gothia.

According to the church historian Philostorgius, the Goths sent Ulfilas as an ambassador to the Roman Empire during the reign of Constantine I, and the Arian Eusebius of Nicomedia consecrated him bishop of Gothia. He mastered Greek and Latin and wrote theological treatises in both. After he returned to Gothia in 341 he spent seven years explaining the Arian doctrine to adherents and to the unconverted. In 348 a Thervingian iudex began a persecution of Christians, and Ulfilas and his followers were expelled and fled to the Roman provinces, where Constantius II accepted them. He settled near Nicopolis in Moesia Inferior and served as bishop there for thirty-three years.

In Moesia he attended church councils, including the Council of Constantinople in 360, where he represented the Moesian Goths. In 380 Theodosius I issued a law against heresy, and the Arian bishops were condemned after the Second Ecumenical Council. Ordered to attend a disputation, Ulfilas travelled to Constantinople, probably in 383, where he fell ill and died, though not before drafting a creed. He was succeeded by Selenas.

Cassiodorus recorded that Ulfilas invented the Gothic letters and translated the scriptures into Gothic. He devised the Gothic alphabet largely from the Greek alphabet, with Latin and runic characters. The traditional date for completing the Bible translation is around 369, but there is no primary evidence that he translated it himself, and analysis of the Gothic text indicates a team of translators, possibly under his supervision. The Creed of Ulfilas, preserved in a letter by his pupil Auxentius of Durostorum, distinguishes God the Father, unbegotten, from the only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, who is subject to the Son.
ulises-heureaux: Ulises Hilarión Heureaux Leibert, nicknamed Lilís, was born in Puerto Plata on 21 October 1845. His father, José D'Assás Heureaux Fortune, was born in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, the son of a judge of the civil court there and a member of his household staff; his mother, Josefa Leibert, was born on the island of Saint Thomas. He spoke French and English fluently as well as Spanish. In the rebellion that followed the Spanish annexation of 1861 he became the principal lieutenant of Gregorio Luperón. In 1876 he organised an uprising that seized Puerto Plata and led to the election of Ulises Espaillat.

When Luperón became president in 1879 and stayed in Puerto Plata, he delegated authority in Santo Domingo to Heureaux. Under the priest Fernando Meriño, president from September 1880, Heureaux was interior minister, and Meriño handed the government to him on 1 September 1882. In 1884 Luperón backed General Segundo Imbert as successor; Heureaux promised to respect the result but had ballot boxes stuffed for General Francisco Gregorio Billini. Billini was driven to resign on 16 May 1885. In the 1886 election the fraud committed by Heureaux was so blatant that supporters of his opponent, Casimiro de Moya, rose in the Cibao Valley, and he suppressed the rising brutally.

In 1888 he exiled Luperón, and the next year he forced Congress to abolish the bar on presidential re-election and to end direct elections. He brought members of both rival factions, the Rojos and the Azules, into his government, and kept an extensive network of secret police and informants, assassinating or exiling the politicians he could not co-opt. Cuban planters who arrived after the Ten Years' War received large tracts of the southeastern coastal plain and built the country's first mechanised sugar mills. His government electrified Santo Domingo, bridged the Ozama River and began a railway from Santiago to Puerto Plata.

In 1888 he borrowed three-quarters of a million pounds sterling from the Amsterdam house of Westendorp, which went bankrupt in 1892. The San Domingo Improvement Co. of New York bought out its claims. In 1897, with the country near bankruptcy, he printed five million dollars of unsecured paper money, the papeletas de Lilís, which ruined many merchants and helped to provoke a revolt among the tobacco planters and merchants of the Cibao. He was killed by Ramón Cáceres on 26 July 1899. The national debt then exceeded 35 million dollars, fifteen times the annual budget; the government declared bankruptcy, and the American military intervened.
ulpian: Ulpian gave his own origin as Tyre in Roman Syria, in a passage preserved in Justinian I's Digest, compiled in 530 to 533 CE. There he describes Tyre as a splendid colony, loyal in its treaty with the Romans, to which Septimius Severus had granted Italian law. He was most active as a writer between 211 and 222 CE.

He first appears in public life as assessor in the auditorium of Papinian and as a member of the council of Septimius Severus. Under Caracalla he was master of the requests (magister libellorum). Elagabalus banished him from Rome, but on the accession of Severus Alexander in 222 he was reinstated and became the emperor's chief adviser and praetorian prefect. He owned a luxurious villa at Santa Marinella, on the coast north of Rome.

His works include Ad Sabinum, a commentary on the ius civile in over 50 books, and Ad edictum, a commentary on the Edict in 83 books. He also wrote collections of opinions, responses and disputations, books of rules and institutions, and treatises on the functions of the different magistrates. One of these, De officio proconsulis in ten books, is a comprehensive exposition of the criminal law. Further monographs deal with statutes and with testamentary trusts.

His writings supplied about a third of the contents of Justinian's Digest, and his commentary on the Edict alone about a fifth. He is described as an author of high doctrinal exposition, judicious in criticism and lucid in arrangement, style and language. He is also credited with the first life table. He is remembered for the principle that the precepts of law are to live honourably, not to harm any other person, and to render each his own.

By curtailing the privileges that Elagabalus had granted to the Praetorian Guard, Ulpian earned its enmity and narrowly escaped its vengeance once. He was finally murdered in the palace by the Guard, in the presence of the emperor, possibly in the course of a riot between the soldiers and the mob. The year of his death cannot be determined with certainty. Robert Lee Cleve argues for 223, citing a papyrus discovered in 1966, while 228 has also been proposed. Scholars today agree that the grammarian Ulpian in Athenaeus's Deipnosophists is not the historical jurist, but possibly his father.
ulugh-beg: Ulugh Beg was born on 22 March 1394 in Sultaniyeh, during his grandfather Timur's invasion of Persia, and was named Mīrzā Muhammad Tāraghay. He was the eldest son of Shah Rukh and Gawhar Shad. Ulugh Beg, meaning roughly Great Ruler, was a title and not a personal name; it is the Turkic equivalent of Timur's title Amīr-e Kabīr.

As a child he travelled through much of the Middle East and India as Timur extended his conquests. After Timur's death Shah Rukh moved the capital to Herat, and in 1409 the sixteen-year-old Ulugh Beg became governor of Samarkand. In 1411 he was named sovereign ruler of the whole of Mavarannahr.

Ulugh Beg set out to make Samarkand an intellectual centre. Between 1417 and 1420 he built a madrasa on Registan Square and invited astronomers and mathematicians to teach there, among them Qadi Zada al-Rumi and later Jamshid al-Kashi. His best-known pupil in astronomy was Ali Qushchi. He built an observatory in Samarkand between 1424 and 1429, whose largest instrument, the Fakhri sextant, had a radius of about 36 metres. With it he compiled a star catalogue, the Zij-i-Sultani, based on new observations, which is generally considered the best between those of Ptolemy and Tycho Brahe.

He measured the length of the sidereal year and the Earth's axial tilt, and wrote trigonometric tables of sines and tangents correct to at least eight decimal places. He also kept up diplomacy with the Ming dynasty, exchanging envoys with the Yongle emperor from 1416. His military record was weaker. A campaign against Moghulistan in 1425 left its ruler Shir Muhammad in power, and in 1427 his army was defeated by Baraq, Khan of the Golden Horde, near Sighnaq. It was the last campaign he led against a neighbouring power.

On the death of Shah Rukh in 1447, Ulugh Beg marched against his nephew Ala al-Dawla, who had claimed rule at Herat, and was defeated there in 1448 by Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza. His eldest son Abdal-Latif Mirza then rebelled against him at Balkh, and Ulugh Beg surrendered to him at Samarkand.

Abdal-Latif allowed him to set out on pilgrimage to Mecca but had him assassinated in 1449. His nephew Abdallah Mirza later restored his reputation and placed his remains at Timur's feet in the Gur-e-Amir, where Soviet archaeologists found them in 1941. A crater on the Moon, named by Johann Heinrich von Mädler on his 1830 map, and the asteroid 2439 Ulugbek bear his name.
ulugh-khan: Ulugh Khan was originally named Almas Beg. His father, Shihabuddin Mas'ud, was the elder brother of Sultan Jalaluddin, founder of the Khalji dynasty, and both Almas Beg and his elder brother Alauddin married daughters of Jalaluddin. Under Jalaluddin he held the post of Akhur-beg, equivalent to master of the horse. In 1296, after Alauddin had raided Devagiri and kept the loot, Almas Beg assured the sultan of his brother's loyalty and persuaded him to visit Kara, where Alauddin killed him on 20 July 1296. The new sultan made his brother barbeg with the title Ulugh Khan, meaning Great Khan. He also held the iqta' of Bayana.

In November 1296 Alauddin sent him and Zafar Khan with an army of 30,000 to 40,000 against Multan, held by Jalaluddin's son Arkali Khan. After two months of siege the leaders of the defence went over to Delhi. Ulugh Khan promised Arkali Khan and his brother Ruknuddin Ibrahim that they would not be harmed, but imprisoned them once the city was occupied; they were later blinded or killed by Nusrat Khan on Alauddin's orders. According to the courtier Amir Khusrau, he reached the Sutlej River on 6 February 1298 and defeated the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate there, with 20,000 Mongol dead.

On the way back from Gujarat in 1299, near Jalore, he and Nusrat Khan punished soldiers for withholding the khums, the fifth of the loot due to the treasury. Recently converted Mongol soldiers mutinied; some 2,000 to 3,000 attacked his camp and killed a nephew of Alauddin whom they took for him. Against Hammira of Ranthambore in 1301 he defeated and killed the general Bhimasimha at the Banas River, but after Nusrat Khan was killed in the siege he was forced back to Jhain, and Alauddin came in person and took the fort in July 1301.

Ordered to prepare a march on the Kakatiya capital Warangal, he assembled a large army but died a few months later. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani writes that Alauddin was greatly depressed and gave much in charity for his brother's soul. Barani's contemporary Isami claims instead that Alauddin had him poisoned, suspecting that he had been ready to take the throne when the sultan was wrongly reported dead; later chroniclers repeat this. The historian Banarsi Prasad Saksena dismisses Isami's account as false, while Kishori Saran Lal thinks it not impossible. Claims that he led the invasion of Gujarat in 1304, or governed it for 20 years, are of doubtful accuracy.
ulysses-s-grant: Grant was born Hiram Ulysses Grant on 27 April 1822, the first child of Jesse Root Grant, a Whig supporter and fervent abolitionist, and Hannah Simpson. The family moved to Georgetown, Ohio, in 1823. When Representative Thomas L. Hamer nominated him to the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1839, Hamer altered his name, and he was enlisted as U. S. Grant. He served in the Mexican–American War and married Julia Dent on 22 August 1848. After resigning in 1854 he had no trade, and seven years of financial struggle followed; he farmed near St. Louis and sold firewood on its street corners.

When the Civil War began in April 1861 Grant became colonel of the 21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment. His victories in the western theatre in 1862 brought him prominence, and in 1863 his Vicksburg campaign gave Union forces control of the Mississippi River. After Chattanooga, Abraham Lincoln promoted him to lieutenant general and command of all Union armies. Grant fought Robert E. Lee through the Overland Campaign in 1864, and a nine-month siege of Petersburg followed. Lee abandoned Petersburg and Richmond after a general assault ordered on 2 April 1865 and surrendered at Appomattox.

Nominated unanimously by the Republicans in 1868, Grant was sworn in as president on 4 March 1869 and urged ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment. He appointed Ely S. Parker, a Seneca, as Commissioner of Indian Affairs, the first Native American in the post. His second term was beset by scandals, and the Panic of 1873 began the Long Depression. Leaving office in 1877, he toured the world for about two and a half years, meeting Queen Victoria, Otto von Bismarck, Li Hongzhang and Emperor Meiji.

Grant failed to win the Republican nomination for a third term in 1880. His savings were depleted, and a railway venture in Mexico went bankrupt in 1884. That autumn he learned that a sore throat was cancer, possibly caused by his frequent cigar smoking, and he wrote his memoirs as he was dying. He died on 23 July 1885. At his death he was the most popular American and was memorialised as a symbol of national unity. His reputation suffered for a time under the Lost Cause mythology spread by Confederate sympathisers around the turn of the twentieth century.
umar-ibn-abd-al-aziz: Umar was probably born in Medina. His father, Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, belonged to the ruling Umayyad family, and his mother, Layla bint Asim, was a granddaughter of the second Rashidun caliph Umar. Historians later stressed this descent to set his character apart from other Umayyad caliphs. His father governed Egypt from 685, and Umar spent part of his childhood there before being educated in Medina, where he formed ties with pious men and transmitters of hadith.

Al-Walid I appointed him governor of Medina in 706, with his jurisdiction later extended to Mecca and Taif. Traditional accounts call him a just governor. From 707 he rebuilt and enlarged the Prophet's Mosque. The Hejaz became a refuge for Iraqi exiles fleeing al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who pressured the caliph to dismiss Umar in 712. He stayed at court and became a principal adviser to Sulayman.

According to the traditional sources, Sulayman on his deathbed at Dabiq was persuaded by Raja ibn Haywa to name Umar as his successor, though Reinhard Eisener thinks Raja's role overstated. The choice passed over the descendants of Abd al-Malik, and Umar averted conflict by naming Yazid II as his own successor. He acceded on 22 September 717 and overhauled the provincial administrations, appointing governors for their reliability and integrity.

His most significant reform was the equality of Arab and non-Arab Muslims. Converts no longer paid the jizya, but their land became the property of their villages and stayed liable to the full kharaj, a safeguard against collapse of revenue. He restricted the appropriation of crown lands as private estates and is credited with ordering the first official collection of hadith. Because of the cost of campaigns and the losses at Constantinople, he withdrew the army from the siege, though Muslim forces in al-Andalus conquered and fortified Narbonne in his reign.

Umar fell ill on a journey and died between 5 and 10 February 720 at Dayr Sim'an near Maarat al-Numan, where he was buried in a plot he had bought with his own funds. Yazid II succeeded him. Muslim tradition is unanimous, in Hugh Kennedy's words, that he was pious and ruled like a true Muslim, unlike the other Umayyads. He was widely regarded in Medina as the Mahdi, and many Muslims count him the fifth rightly guided caliph. The Abbasids spared his body from the desecration they applied to other Umayyad caliphs. Kennedy calls him the most puzzling of the Marwanid rulers.
umar-ibn-al-khattab: Umar was born in Mecca, a member of the Banu Adi, a minor clan of the Quraysh, and later became its leader. Unusually among the Quraysh, he learned to read and write, and he appreciated poetry. He at first opposed Muhammad and the new faith and even set out to kill him, but on the way was turned aside by a clansman who told him that his own sister Fatima bint al-Khattab and her husband had secretly become Muslims. Umar converted in 616 and then became the first Muslim to pray openly in the Kaaba. He took part in nearly all of Muhammad's battles, and Muhammad gave him the title al-Fārūq, the Distinguisher.

After Muhammad's death on 8 June 632, Umar helped bring about Abu Bakr's election at the gathering at Saqifa, and he served Abu Bakr as chief adviser. He urged that the Quran be compiled into a single volume after the Battle of al-Yamama. Abu Bakr named him successor, over the objection of Talha ibn Ubayd Allah that Umar was too severe. Umar was the first to take the title amir al-mu'minin, Commander of the Faithful.

Under him the caliphate expanded across Syria, Egypt, Iraq, the Jazira and deep into Persia. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas commanded against the Sasanians in Iraq, where the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah led to the fall of Mesopotamia, and Amr ibn al-As led the conquest of Egypt. The Sasanian state was shattered at the Battle of Nahavand. Umar dismissed the successful general Khalid ibn al-Walid, reportedly to show that victory comes from God and to check a cult of personality around him.

Umar picked provincial governors for ability rather than tribal standing, and never appointed one for more than two years, so that none gathered too much local power. He set up a cabinet and formalised the Bayt al-mal, the central treasury at Medina, with provincial branches. Jews and Christians continued under their own legal and judicial arrangements. He is credited with canal works in Basra and a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea.

In 644 Umar was assassinated by a Persian slave, Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz. His motive is unclear, though medieval sources point to a tax dispute with his master al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba. Sources differ on whether the assassin was executed or killed himself. Umar left no clear successor. Sunni Muslims revere him as a just ruler and the second of the rightly guided caliphs, remembered for his plain living, while Shia Muslims view him negatively.
umar-marvi: The tale is said to date back to the 14th century and probably originated in the Soomra period, between 1050 and 1350. It was first written down in the 16th century by Shah Abdul Karim of Bulri, the great-great-grandfather of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, in his Bayan ul Arifeen, known to Sindhis as Karim Jo Risalo. It also appears in two chronicles, the Tarikh-i Tahiri, compiled in 1621, and the Tuhfat-al-Kiram of 1766–67.

In the story as it is told, Marvi is a young Khaskheli girl of the Panhwar tribe, and her captor is Umar Soomro, then ruler of Umerkot, who wanted to marry her for her beauty. When she refused him she was held for several years in Umarkot Fort. She resists both the ruler's overtures and the temptation to live in the palace as a queen, preferring a simple rural life among her own village people.

In the Shah Jo Risalo the tale stands among seven popular tragic romances of Sindh, with Sassui Punnhun, Sohni Mehar, Lilan Chanesar, Noori Jam Tamachi, Sorath Rai Diyach and Momal Rano. Their heroines are commonly known as the Seven Queens of Sindh, or the seven heroines of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Marvi is regarded, for her courage, as a symbol of love for one's soil.

The story has been retold in modern forms. A film, Umar Marvi, directed by Shaikh Hassan and produced by Syed Hussain Ali Shah Fazlani, who also acted in it, was released on 12 March 1956 as the first Sindhi-language feature film made in Pakistan. The Pakistan Television Corporation broadcast a serial, Marvi, in 1993, which set the story in modern times. The Indian writer Ram Panjwani wrote a Sindhi play, Umar Marui, and a Sindhi song of Coke Studio's fifteenth season, Aayi Aayi, was inspired by the tale.
umayyad-caliphate: Before Islam the Banu Umayya were a leading clan of the Quraysh of Mecca, dominating its trade with Syria. Under Abu Sufyan ibn Harb they led the Meccan opposition to the Prophet Muhammad, but after Muhammad captured Mecca in 630, Abu Sufyan and the Quraysh embraced Islam. The third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, was also an Umayyad. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, long the governor of Syria, became caliph in 661 after emerging victorious in the First Fitna, and Damascus became the capital.

During the Second Fitna the Sufyanid line of Mu'awiya was replaced in 684 by Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who won the Battle of Marj Rahit that August. His son Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan defeated the Zubayrids in 692, centralised power and pursued Arabization of the bureaucracy; government records, kept until then in Greek, Coptic and Persian, began to be written in Arabic. The Umayyads conquered the Maghreb, the Iberian Peninsula, Central Asia and Sindh, and at its largest the caliphate covered 11,000,000 to 15,000,000 square kilometres.

Hisham (r. 724–743) curtailed expansion. Constant warfare exhausted the caliphate, and discontent among non-Arab converts, who lacked the rights of Arab Muslims, helped cause the Abbasid revolution of the 740s. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew Marwan II and most of the Umayyad family was slain. In 756 Abd al-Rahman I, a grandson of Hisham, founded an independent state in al-Andalus with its capital at Córdoba.

The early caliphs followed Byzantine administrative practice, with branches for political affairs, military affairs, tax collection and religious administration, and governors appointed by the caliph in each province. The army was mainly Arab and salaried. The Umayyads minted the first coins struck by a Muslim government. Society had four classes: Arab Muslims, non-Arab Muslim clients, dhimmis such as Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, who paid the jizya tax, and slaves. Christians, still the majority of the population, held prominent administrative posts under the early caliphs. Umayyad monuments include the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem and the Great Mosque of Damascus.
umayyad-mosque: The site has been a place of worship since the Iron Age, when the Arameans of Aram-Damascus built a temple to Hadad-Ramman, god of thunderstorms and rain. Under the Seleucids it was dedicated to Zeus, and after Roman conquest of Damascus in 64 BCE it became a temple of Jupiter, enlarged probably from the reign of Augustus. The Roman temenos walls still form the outer walls of the mosque.

Emperor Theodosius I turned the temple into a cathedral. After the Muslim conquest of Damascus in 634 a prayer room, a musalla, was set up in part of the building, and the Christians kept the rest. Al-Walid I, the sixth Umayyad caliph, took over the cathedral, returning other properties in the city to the Christians as compensation.

The mosque was built over nine years by thousands of labourers and artisans from the Islamic and Byzantine worlds, paid for from the war booty of Umayyad conquests and taxes on the Arab troops of Damascus. Al-Walid supervised the work and told the people of Damascus that he wished to add a fifth distinction to their climate, water, fruits and baths: this mosque. The plan has a large courtyard on the north, measuring with the whole complex 97 by 156 metres, and a prayer hall along the south wall with three parallel aisles crossed by a central nave leading to the mihrab.

The architect re-used the columns and arcades of the church. Gold mosaics of vegetal motifs covered some 4,000 square metres and are likely the largest in the world. Later rulers added to it. The Abbasid governor built the Dome of the Treasury in 789–90, and a minaret, the Minaret of the Bride, is credited to the reign of al-Ma'mun. Baybars ordered extensive restoration of its marble, mosaics and gilding in 1270, and the Mamluks added the Minaret of Qaitbay.

Medieval Muslim writers regarded the mosque as a wonder of the world. It is considered the oldest mosque still in use in its original form, and one of the few early mosques to keep the general structure of the early 8th century. Its plan has served as a model for congregational mosques, among them al-Azhar and the Baybars Mosque in Cairo, the Great Mosque of Cordoba and the Grand Mosques of Bursa and Edirne.

Christians and Muslims alike hold that the head of John the Baptist is buried there, a tradition from the 6th century, and two shrines commemorate Husayn ibn Ali. One hadith places the descent of Jesus at a white minaret in Damascus, which tradition identifies with the Minaret of Isa; most Muslim theologians read this symbolically.
umberto-i: Umberto was born in Turin on 14 March 1844, the son of Victor Emmanuel II and Archduchess Adelaide of Austria. His father distrusted him and gave him no training in politics or constitutional government; he was taught to be obedient and had to kiss his father's hand before speaking to him. From March 1858 he had a military career in the Royal Sardinian Army.

He was present at the battle of Solferino in 1859 and in 1866 commanded the XVI Division at Villafranca after the Italian defeat at Custoza. On 21 April 1868 he married his first cousin Margherita of Savoy, whose cultural interests and strong personality enhanced the popularity of the monarchy. Their only son was the future Victor Emmanuel III.

Umberto came to the throne on 9 January 1878 and took the title Umberto I of Italy. In November of that year the anarchist Giovanni Passannante attacked him with a dagger during a parade in Naples; the king warded off the blow with his sabre. He approved the Triple Alliance with Austria-Hungary and Germany, formalised in 1882, though many in Italy were hostile to an alliance with their former Austrian enemies. A strong militarist, he backed colonial expansion, which began in 1885 with the occupation of Massawa in Eritrea, and Italy also expanded into Somalia.

In December 1893 he appointed Francesco Crispi prime minister, who governed in an authoritarian manner. Italian forces were defeated at the Battle of Adwa in Ethiopia on 1 March 1896, which led to demonstrations in Rome. Social unrest grew late in his reign, with the spread of socialism and crackdowns on civil liberties. On 7 May 1898, during demonstrations over the price of bread, General Fiorenzo Bava Beccaris put Milan under military rule and ordered rifle fire and artillery against the crowds. The authorities counted 82 dead, and opposition sources claimed 400. Umberto telegraphed his congratulations and later decorated the general, which outraged much of public opinion.

On the evening of 29 July 1900, as the king returned from a military parade in Monza, the Italian-American anarchist Gaetano Bresci shot him in the chest, neck and left thigh. Contemporary reports and later scholarship give Bresci's motive as revenge for the victims of the Bava Beccaris massacre. Bresci said that he had killed not Umberto but the king, a principle.

He was found hanged in his cell on 22 May 1901. Umberto was buried in the Pantheon in Rome next to his father on 9 August 1900, the last member of the House of Savoy buried there, and his son Victor Emmanuel III succeeded him. The Umbertino style of architecture is named after him.
umberto-ii: Umberto was born at the Castle of Racconigi in Piedmont, the third child and only son of King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy and Jelena of Montenegro. Because the Italian throne was limited to male descendants, he was heir apparent from birth, and a Royal Decree of 29 September 1904 formalised his title of Prince of Piedmont. On 24 October 1929, in Brussels, on the day his betrothal was announced, Fernando de Rosa fired a single shot at him with a cry of 'Down with Mussolini!' and missed. He married Princess Marie José of Belgium in Rome on 8 January 1930, and they had four children.

Umberto became commander-in-chief of the Northern Armies and then the Southern ones, but the post was formal, since his father guarded the supreme command from Benito Mussolini. In June 1940 he ostensibly commanded Army Group West in the Italian invasion of France. The offensive went only a few kilometres into French territory, and his reputation was saved only because the defeated French signed an armistice with Italy on 24 June 1940. Promoted Marshal of Italy in 1942, he turned against the war after the defeats at Stalingrad and El Alamein. In September 1943 he reluctantly obeyed his father's order to flee Rome for the south, reaching Brindisi on 9 September, and for the first time openly criticised him.

In 1944 Victor Emmanuel III, compromised by his ties to Fascism, transferred his powers to Umberto, who became Lieutenant General of the Realm. After the liberation of Rome on 6 June 1944 the political parties pressed him to dismiss Pietro Badoglio as prime minister, and Ivanoe Bonomi was appointed. The king abdicated on 9 May 1946 in the hope of strengthening the monarchy before the institutional referendum. Umberto's reign lasted 34 days, until his formal deposition on 12 June 1946, and earned him the name May King. Voters chose to abolish the monarchy.

He spent the next 37 years in exile at Cascais in Portugal. The 1948 constitution barred male heirs of the defunct throne from Italian soil until 2002. He died in Geneva on 18 March 1983 and was interred at Hautecombe Abbey in France, the burial place of the House of Savoy for centuries.
umbria: Umbria is the only Italian region with neither a coastline nor a border with another country. It lies between Tuscany, Marche and Lazio, includes part of the central Apennines, and is crossed by the Tiber. Its capital is Perugia. In antiquity a pair of shallow lakes, the Lacus Clitorius and the Lacus Umber, covered the plain; the Romans drained them, an earthquake in the 4th century let the basin refill, and Benedictine monks began draining it again in the 13th century, a work completed in the 18th.

The region is named for the Umbri, an Italic people who spoke Umbrian, a language related to Latin and Oscan. Unlike the Etruscans, they mostly lived in small dwellings in the Apennines. The Etruscans, their chief enemies, drove them towards the uplands from about 700 to 500 BCE, with the Tiber as the border. The Iguvine Tablets of Gubbio, written in Umbrian around the turn of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, are the longest and most important document of the Osco-Umbrian languages.

Rome defeated the Samnites and their Gallic allies at Sentinum in 295 BCE, which began a period of integration; the Romans founded colonies such as Spoletium and built the Via Flaminia in 219 BCE. Perugia took Mark Antony's side in 40 BCE and was almost completely destroyed by Octavian. After Rome's fall, Ostrogoths and Byzantines fought over the region, and the Lombards founded the Duchy of Spoleto.

When Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdoms, some Umbrian territories passed to the Pope. Cities gained autonomy as comuni, and families such as the Baglioni in Perugia held power as signori. By the middle of the 14th century Cardinal Albornoz had brought the region into the Papal States, and the papacy ruled it uncontested until the end of the 18th century. Umbria was part of the Napoleonic Empire from 1809 to 1814 as the department of Trasimène. In 1860 the people of Perugia destroyed the Rocca Paolina, the fortress Pope Paul III had built there, in the year the region was annexed by Victor Emmanuel II.

Umbria is divided into the provinces of Perugia and Terni. Assisi, associated with Saint Francis, is a World Heritage Site. Gubbio holds the Festival of the Ceri each 15 May, a race held every year since 1160, and the Ceri appear on the region's coat of arms. Umbria is also where the umber pigment was originally extracted.
umm-kulthum: Fatima Ibrahim es-Sayyid el-Beltagi was born on 4 May 1904 in the village of Tamay ez-Zahayra, in the markaz of Senbellawein. Her father, Ibrahim es-Sayyid el-Beltagi, was a rural imam and her mother, Fatmah el-Maleegi, a housewife. She learned to sing by listening to her father teach her older brother Khalid, and through him she learned to recite the Qur'an, which she reportedly memorised entirely. Her father at first dressed her in boys' clothes when she sang, because singing was unacceptable for girls in the countryside at that time.

Amin El Mahdi invited her into the cultural circles of Cairo. In 1924 she was introduced to the poet Ahmed Rami, who wrote 137 songs for her and became her mentor in Arabic literature. She made her first recordings in 1924 for labels such as Odeon Records, but her recordings of 1927 truly launched her career. She studied with Abu al-Ila Muhammad from her arrival in Cairo until his death in 1927.

Her mature style in the 1940s and early 1950s is known as her golden age. In the early 1940s she asked the composer Zakariya Ahmad and the colloquial poet Mahmud Bayram el-Tunsi for songs in indigenously Egyptian styles, a departure from the romantic songs of the 1930s led by Mohammad El-Qasabgi. Their last stage collaboration was Raq el Habib in 1941. Riad Al-Sunbati became a main composer.

Around 1965 she began working with Mohammed Abdel Wahab, whose first song for her was Inta Omri. After the Six-Day War of 1967 her songs became more reflective, and she gave concerts in several Arab and European countries to raise funds for the Egyptian war effort under the slogan Art for the War Effort. She also appeared in six films, including Weddad in 1936 and Sallama in 1945.

By the late 1940s she was affected by Graves' disease, and in 1953 she travelled to the United States for surgery. She resumed singing in 1954 and wore heavy sunglasses thereafter. That year she married Dr Hasan al-Hifnawi; they had no children. She died on 3 February 1975 of kidney failure, aged 70.

About 4 million people lined the streets for her funeral procession from the Omar Makram mosque, and mourners took her coffin from its bearers and carried it to the Al Azhar mosque. She was buried near the Mausoleum of Imam al-Shafi'i in the City of the Dead in Cairo. In Egypt she is called Elsett, the Lady, and a museum in Cairo holds her belongings.
uncle-toms-cabin: Harriet Beecher Stowe, a Connecticut-born teacher at the Hartford Female Seminary, belonged to the religious Beecher family and was an active abolitionist. She wrote a sentimental novel to depict the horrors of slavery while asserting that Christian love could overcome it. It first appeared as a 40-week serial in The National Era, an abolitionist periodical, from 5 June 1851 to 1 April 1852. It was meant to run for only a few weeks, but Stowe expanded it, and protests reached the office when she missed an issue. The character of Eliza was inspired by an account of a slave woman who crossed the frozen Ohio River in February 1838.

The book opens in Kentucky, where the farmer Arthur Shelby, facing the loss of his farm through debt, sells two of his slaves to the slave trader Mr. Haley: Uncle Tom, a middle-aged man with a wife and children, and Harry, the young son of Emily Shelby's maid Eliza. Eliza overhears the plan and flees with her son across the ice of the Ohio River. Tom is taken down the river to New Orleans, and after his owner St. Clare dies, he is sold to the plantation owner Simon Legree.

Legree beats Tom when he refuses to whip a fellow slave, and tries to crush his faith, but Tom keeps reading his Bible and comforting the others. Eliza's family reaches Canada, then France and Liberia, and George Shelby frees the slaves of the Kentucky farm. Stowe's central theme is the evil of slavery, above all the separation of families, together with the power of Christian love.

It was the best-selling novel and second best-selling book of the 19th century in the United States, after the Bible, and it is credited with helping fuel the abolitionist cause. Defenders of slavery protested, and seven Anti-Tom novels appeared in 1852 and six more in 1853. A story that Abraham Lincoln greeted Stowe in 1862 with the words 'So this is the little lady who started this great war' is likely apocryphal. Far more Americans saw the story on stage than read it, in 'Tom shows' such as George L. Aiken's version, the most popular play in the United States and Britain for 75 years.

The novel is a landmark of protest literature, and later books such as The Jungle by Upton Sinclair and Silent Spring by Rachel Carson owe it a large debt. It has also been criticised for racist descriptions of its black characters and for stereotypes it helped fix, and the Tom of the title came to mean an excessively subservient person. James Baldwin, in 1945, called it a bad novel.
unesco: The organisation's mandate for international cooperation can be traced to a League of Nations resolution of 21 September 1921, which asked for a commission to study whether nations could freely share cultural, educational and scientific achievements. The resulting International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation was created in 1922. Its members included Henri Bergson, Albert Einstein, Marie Curie, Robert A. Millikan and Gonzague de Reynold, and it was a small body centred largely on Western Europe.

The International Institute for Intellectual Cooperation was set up in Paris in September 1924 as the committee's executing agency. The International Bureau of Education began work in December 1925 as a non-governmental body; it formed a joint commission with UNESCO in 1952 and joined it in 1969. World War II largely interrupted the work of the predecessor bodies, and UNESCO was founded in 1945 as their successor.

UNESCO is governed by a General Conference of member states and associate members, which meets every two years to set its programmes and budget. The conference elects an executive board of 58 members who hold office for four years, and appoints a Director-General every four years. The headquarters stand at the Place de Fontenoy in Paris, built by a group of architects including Bernard Zehrfuss, Marcel Breuer and Luigi Nervi. The grounds hold a Garden of Peace, given by the government of Japan and designed by Isamu Noguchi in 1958.

Its work falls under five programme areas: education, natural sciences, social and human sciences, culture, and communication and information. It adopted the Convention against Discrimination in Education in 1960 and the Seville Statement on Violence in 1989, and it designates places and projects of significance, among them biosphere reserves, begun in 1971, and the Memory of the World register, begun in 1997.

In the 1970s and 1980s UNESCO's support for a New World Information and Communication Order was condemned in the United States, the United Kingdom and Singapore as an attempt to curb freedom of the press. The United States withheld its contributions and withdrew in 1984, and the United Kingdom followed in 1985. Singapore also left at the end of 1985, citing rising membership fees. The United Kingdom rejoined after a change of government in 1997, the United States in 2003 and Singapore on 8 October 2007.
unesco-world-heritage-site: The programme grew out of a rescue operation. In 1954 the government of Egypt decided to build the Aswan High Dam, whose reservoir would flood a stretch of the Nile valley containing the cultural treasures of ancient Egypt and ancient Nubia. In 1960 UNESCO's Director-General launched the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia, which led to the excavation and recording of hundreds of sites and the relocation of several temples, among them Abu Simbel and Philae. Its success led to campaigns for Venice, the ruins of Mohenjo-daro and the Borobodur Temple Compounds.
The Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted by the General Conference of UNESCO on 16 November 1972 and came into force on 17 December 1975.

A site is nominated by its host country and decided on by UNESCO's World Heritage Committee, whose 21 states parties are elected by the United Nations General Assembly.
