The name Utah comes from the Spanish Yuta, recorded from the 17th century and borrowed from the name of the Ute, a people whose name for themselves is Núuchi-u. It is commonly said to mean people of the mountains.

Francisco Vázquez de Coronado explored southern Utah in 1540 while looking for Cíbola. A group led by two Catholic priests, the Domínguez-Escalante expedition, left Santa Fe in 1776 hoping to find a route to California and travelled as far north as Utah Lake. In 1821, the year Mexico became independent, the region became part of its territory of Alta California.

Many early settlers, even under Mexico, came from the United States, among them Mormons fleeing persecution. In 1848, after the Mexican-American War, the region was annexed by the United States and became Utah Territory. Disputes between the Mormon community and Congress delayed statehood until 1896, when, after Utah agreed to outlaw polygamy, it was admitted as the 45th state.

The capital is Salt Lake City, on the Wasatch Front. The 2020 census counted 3,271,616 people. Slightly over half of Utahns are Mormons, mostly members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which has its world headquarters in Salt Lake City, and Utah is the only state where a majority belongs to a single church.
uthman-ibn-affan: Uthman was born in Mecca around 576 into the Banu Abd Shams clan of the Quraysh and its leading family, the Banu Umayya, then the most powerful family of the Quraysh. According to the account of the 9th-century scholar Ibn Sa'd, he became the fourth convert to Islam, and Ibn Ishaq holds that Abu Bakr brought him to Muhammad.

Under pressure from the Quraysh he migrated to Abyssinia with his wife Ruqayya, a daughter of Muhammad, in April 615, and in 622 the couple were among the third group of Muslims to migrate to Medina. His marriages to two of Muhammad's daughters, Ruqayya and Umm Kulthum, earned him the title Dhu al-Nurayn, the Possessor of Two Lights.

Before dying, the caliph Umar appointed a council of six early companions, among them Uthman and Ali ibn Abi Talib, to choose his successor, and Uthman, then aged 68, was elected. His rule saw expansion into Persia, as far as Khorasan and Transoxiana, and westward to Ifriqiya, and he delegated military authority to kinsmen such as Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. In 649 Mu'awiya was allowed to set up a navy, which defeated the Byzantine fleet at the Battle of the Masts in 655.

Around 650, noticing differences in how the Qur'an was recited as Islam spread, he ordered a committee headed by Zayd ibn Thabit to prepare a standard text from the copy kept by Hafsa bint Umar. Copies were sent to the main cities and other versions were ordered burnt. Shi'a Muslims use the same Qur'an but do not believe it was first compiled by Uthman.

Discontent grew over his fiscal policies and his appointment of relatives to office. Around 654 he called his twelve provincial governors to Medina, and rebel contingents of about 1,000 each came from Egypt, Kufa and Basra. They besieged his house; his supporters, who outnumbered them, asked to fight, but he refused in order to avoid bloodshed among Muslims. On 17 June 656 rebels climbed in from a neighbouring house and killed him as he recited the Qur'an. Sunni tradition counts him the third rightly guided caliph, and Sunni historians view his rule positively, particularly his leniency. Others accuse him of corruption.
uwajima: Uwajima lies in southwestern Ehime Prefecture, facing a wide rias coastline and remote islands on Uwa Bay, with mountains on its other three sides. It covers 468.19 square kilometres and has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers and cool winters, and its heaviest rain falls from June to September. It neighbours Ainan, Kihoku, Matsuno and Seiyo in Ehime and Shimanto and Sukumo in Kōchi Prefecture. Many people think of it as the westernmost city in Ehime, although Yawatahama lies to its north-northwest.

The area belonged to ancient Iyo Province. In the Heian period Uwajima Bay, notably the island of Hiburijima, was a centre of piracy in the Seto Inland Sea and the stronghold of Fujiwara no Sumitomo in his rebellion. In the Muromachi period the Ashikaga shogunate appointed a branch of the Saionji family as governor. It was repeatedly attacked by stronger neighbours, among them Ouchi Yoshitaka, Mōri Motonari, Ōtomo Sōrin and the Chōsokabe, and was overcome by Chōsokabe Motochika, who was in turn overthrown by the forces of Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

After Hideyoshi's settlement of Iyo, Toda Katsutaka held the area. He ruled with extreme harshness, and when ordered to send troops to the invasion of Korea in 1592 he cut down large trees in shrines and temples to build ships. He died in Korea without an heir. Hideyoshi then gave the domain to Tōdō Takatora, a noted castle designer who spent six years building Itajima Castle, later called Uwajima Castle. In 1614 Date Hidemune, the eldest son of Date Masamune by a concubine, was awarded the 100,000 koku Uwajima Domain by the shogun Tokugawa Hidetada, and moved into the castle the following year. His descendants ruled the domain until the Meiji restoration.

The modern town of Uwajima was created after the restoration and was raised to city status on 1 August 1921 after merging with the village of Yahata. Bombing in 1945 destroyed much of the centre, but reconstruction was rapid. Neighbouring villages and, on 1 August 2005, the towns of Mima, Tsushima and Yoshida were merged into the city.

Uwajima is the largest municipality of southwestern Ehime. Its economy rests on commercial fishing, aquaculture and cultured pearls, and it has a single shipyard. Uwajima Castle is one of the 12 Japanese castles with an original donjon from the Edo period. The Date Family Museum holds objects tied to the region and its daimyo family, and Ryūkō-ji and Butsumoku-ji are the 41st and 42nd temples on the Shikoku Pilgrimage. The Ushi-oni Festival, held in July, includes a parade of ushioni teams, dance and a bullfight, in which two bulls fight in a ring until one flees or its knees touch the ground.
uyghurs: The Uyghurs are a Turkic people of Central and East Asia who speak Uyghur, a Karluk language. Their Turkic origin comes mainly from the Karluks and the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which migrated into the region, and their ancestry also draws on the Tocharians and East Iranian peoples who were indigenous there. Scholars hold that the history of the people is contested. Uyghur historians have given the people a very long history, while the official Chinese view dates the ethnic group from the collapse of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840. Many Western scholars do not see the modern Uyghurs as direct descendants of the khaganate, but as descendants of several peoples, one of them the ancient Uyghurs.

The Uyghurs of the khaganate belonged to a Turkic confederation called the Tiele, who lived south of Lake Baikal and around the Yenisei River. The Uyghur Khaganate lasted from 744 to 840 and was governed from Ordu-Baliq, one of the largest ancient cities built in Mongolia. In 840, after a famine and civil war, it was overrun by the Yenisei Kirghiz, and most of its tribal groups dispersed. Some Uyghurs moved to Jimsar, Turpan and Gansu and founded kingdoms, among them the Ganzhou Kingdom (870 to 1036), which was absorbed by the Western Xia. They mixed with the Tocharians of the Tarim Basin and adopted oasis agriculture.

The ancient Uyghurs held many local beliefs, including shamanism and Tengrism, and adopted Manichaeism as the state religion of the khaganate, possibly in 762 or 763; later, in Qocho, many were Buddhists. Inhabitants of the Tarim Basin were gradually converted to Islam after the 10th century, and by the 16th century most identified as Muslims. The region came under the Qing dynasty in the 18th century after the Dzungar–Qing Wars and became the province of Xinjiang. Until 1921 the people of the Tarim Basin used terms such as Kashgarlik and Yarkandlik; in that period Turkic intellectuals meeting in Tashkent adopted the name Uyghur.

Uyghur literature in the Kara-Khanid period is regarded by modern Uyghurs as an important part of their tradition. It includes Yusuf Khass Hajib's Kutadgu Bilig, written in 1069–70, and Mahmud al-Kashgari's dictionary of Turkic dialects of 1072. In the 20th century two short-lived East Turkestan republics were proclaimed, in 1933 and in 1944. Today the Uyghurs are the titular nationality of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in north-western China, one of the country's 55 officially recognised ethnic minorities, and communities live in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkey.
uzbekistan: Uzbekistan has an area of 448,978 square kilometres and stretches 1,425 kilometres from west to east. It is doubly landlocked: none of its rivers reach the sea, since they lie in a series of endorheic basins. It is the only Central Asian state that borders all four of the others. Less than 10% of its territory is intensively cultivated irrigated land in river valleys and oases, and the rest is the vast Kyzylkum Desert and mountains. The climate is continental, with 100 to 200 millimetres of precipitation a year. The highest point is Khazret Sultan at 4,643 metres. The Aral Sea has been largely desiccated by cotton production established in the Soviet era.

During early antiquity the region was inhabited by nomadic Scythian tribes, who built an extensive irrigation system along the rivers when they settled, and cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand emerged as centres of government and high culture. By the fifth century BCE the Bactrian, Sogdian and Tokharian states dominated the region. Sogdian intermediaries became the wealthiest intermediaries in the silk trade between East Asia and the West, which made Bukhara and Samarkand extremely wealthy. Cyrus the Great and later Darius the Great incorporated Bactria and Chorasmia as satrapies, and in 327 BCE Alexander the Great conquered Sogdiana and Bactria, meeting fierce popular resistance. The Kushan Empire replaced the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom in the first century BCE.

In the eighth century the Arabs under Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Transoxiana, the land between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, which soon became a focal point of the Islamic Golden Age. The Mongol invasion of the 13th century destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire, and in the 14th century Timur established the Timurid Empire from here. Samarkand became a centre of science under Ulugh Beg. Turko-Mongol Shaybanids conquered the Timurid lands in the 16th century, and most of Central Asia was gradually incorporated into the Russian Empire in the 19th, with Tashkent the political centre of Russian Turkestan. The Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1924, and independence was declared in 1991.

Uzbekistan is a secular state with a semi-presidential government, made up of 12 regions, Tashkent City and the autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan. Uzbek is the official language and Russian serves as a lingua franca, while Tajik is spoken mainly in the south around Samarkand and Bukhara. Uzbeks form more than 89% of the population, and most people are Muslim. Many of the great monuments of the Timurid period survive in Samarkand. Uzbekistan is a member of the United Nations and the Commonwealth of Independent States.
uzbeks: The Uzbeks are a Turkic people native to Central Asia, and the largest Turkic group in the region. They emerged through the mixing of settled Iranian populations with Turkic and Mongol nomadic groups that entered the region between the 11th and 15th centuries. The name Uzbek seems to have become widely adopted as an ethnonym under Ozbeg Khan, who converted the Golden Horde to Islam, and its origin is disputed.

One view derives it from Oghuz Khagan, also called Oghuz Beg, and another reads it as meaning independent or the lord himself, from the Turkic oz, self, and bek. The name became associated with the region after the conquests of Muhammad Shaybani in the early 16th century. The Shibanid Uzbeks founded several dynasties in Transoxiana and formed a ruling elite over the local Iranian-speaking population, while keeping a Mongol identity.

The region's earlier history shaped the later Uzbeks. Arab armies completed their conquest of the region in the 8th century, and the Arab victory over Chinese armies at the Talas River in 750 fixed its future as an Islamic region. The Mongol invasion established the tradition that a legitimate ruler of any Central Asian state must be a blood descendant of Genghis Khan. Timur emerged in the 1380s as the dominant force in Mawarannahr, though not a descendant of Genghis, and died in 1405 during an invasion of China.

By 1510 the Uzbeks had completed their conquest of Central Asia, including the territory of present-day Uzbekistan. The most powerful of their states was the Khanate of Bukhara, which controlled Mawarannahr, especially the Tashkent region and the Fergana Valley, and northern Afghanistan. A second state, the Khanate of Khiva, was set up in the Khorazm oasis. The Shaybanid dynasty, successors of Muhammad Shaybani, first competed with the Safavid dynasty of Iran for its eastern territory, and the struggle had a religious side, since the Uzbeks were Sunni and Iran was Shia.

The modern Uzbek nation was created in 1924 by the Soviet Union during the national delimitation of Central Asia. It included not only the Shibanid Uzbeks but also Sarts and Tajiks, groups that had not previously identified as Uzbek, by themselves or by others. Uzbekistan declared independence on 31 August 1991. The Uzbek language is a Turkic language of the Karluk branch, written historically and now in Arabic, Latin and Cyrillic scripts, and Uzbeks are predominantly Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school.
uzhhorod: Uzhhorod lies on the Uzh River on the border with Slovakia and near the border with Hungary. The earliest known name is Ungvár, from the Hungarian Ung, the River Uzh, and vár, castle or fortress, which originally referred to a castle outside the city, probably Nevytske Castle. The name Uzhhorod was coined in Slavophile circles in the early 19th century as a literal translation of Ungvár, and the city officially adopted it some time after 1920, under Czechoslovak administration.

Early Slavs, among them the White Croats, settled the area in the second half of the first millennium. According to the medieval chronicle Gesta Hungarorum, the Magyars led by Álmos took the fortress in 895 from its ruler Laborec. Under the Kingdom of Hungary, King Stephen made it the centre of Ung County to guard the north-eastern border. The Mongols of Batu Khan burned the settlement in 1241 and 1242, and King Béla IV granted it town privileges in 1248. Philip Drugeth, whose family received the town from Charles I of Hungary, built Uzhhorod Castle, and from 1430 it was a free royal town.

In 1646 the Union of Ungvár was proclaimed in a ceremony at the castle, and the Greek-Catholic church was established. It became the seat of the Greek Catholic Eparchy in 1780, and the first railway line, to Chop, opened in 1872. According to the 1910 census, 80.3 per cent of its 16,919 inhabitants were Magyars. After the First World War, Subcarpathia was allotted to Czechoslovakia on 10 September 1919, and Uzhhorod became its administrative centre and acquired a new government quarter.

The First Vienna Award of 1938 returned it to Hungary. German troops entered on 19 March 1944, and in May all the Jews, numbering 9,576 in 1941, were deported to Auschwitz and murdered, with only a few hundred surviving. The Red Army captured the city on 27 October 1944, and in 1945 the region was annexed by the Soviet Union and Uzhhorod State University opened.

Since 1991 Uzhhorod has been one of the regional capitals of independent Ukraine, the smallest and westernmost of them, and the centre of Zakarpattia Oblast, which was formed in January 1946. Its university is now Uzhhorod National University. A bust of Tomáš Masaryk, the first president of Czechoslovakia, was unveiled in a main square in 2002, replacing one of 1928 that Hungary removed in 1939.
uzice: Užice lies 411 metres above sea level on both sides of the river Đetinja, surrounded by the Dinaric Alps, and is the administrative centre of the Zlatibor District in western Serbia. The mountain region of Zlatibor, with a long tradition of tourism, lies 25 kilometres to the south. To the west are the mountains Tara and Zvijezda, which together form Tara National Park, covering 220 square kilometres. The Illyrian Parthini and the Celtic-influenced Autariatae settled the region, and in Roman times a municipium called Capedunum stood here; its name points to a Celtic origin.

The first record of Užice by name dates from 1329. Under Emperor Stefan Dušan it is mentioned as a fortress held by the Vojinović family. After the Serbian Empire fell apart, Vojislav Vojinović controlled it, and after him his nephew Nikola Altomanović. Lazar Hrebeljanović and Tvrtko I of Bosnia defeated Nikola and divided his lands, and on Stefan Musić's orders Nikola was blinded in the fortress. Užice then passed to Lazar and to the Serbian Despotate under his son Stefan Lazarević.

Užice fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1463. A first census of 1476 to 1478 listed it as a village, but by the late 15th century the authorities restored the fortress and encouraged settlement, and by the early 16th century it was an administrative capital with a majority Turkish population. Habsburg forces captured it in 1690, and many Serbs left in the Great Migrations of the Serbs. It fell to rebels in the Serbian Revolution but Ottoman forces retook it in 1813. In 1900 a hydroelectric plant on the Đetinja made it the first town in Serbia, and one of the first in Europe, to produce alternating current.

After the Nazi occupation, Yugoslav Partisans liberated Užice in 1941 and made it the capital of the Republic of Užice, which lasted 67 days from 24 September to 29 November 1941, until German forces re-occupied the territory and the Partisans withdrew. After the war the town was renamed Titovo Užice, until 1992.

The Old Town fortress dates from the 14th century. Among its other notable buildings are St. George's Cathedral, St. Mark's Church and the Jokanović house, one of the oldest buildings in the city. The National Museum shows its history. The writer Milutin Uskoković, born in Užice, is described as the author of the first modern novel in Serbia.
